title: Mavrud and the Broad-Leaved Vine: Thrace to Melnik in Harvest Week
subRegion: Thracian Lowlands PGI and the Struma Valley PGI

bestPeriod.window: mid-September to mid-October, *grozdober*, the harvest, when the crush pads are running and the estates are at their most open
bestPeriod.avoid: July-August (40°C on the Thracian plain, cellars shut for holidays) and January-February, when most tasting rooms open by appointment only or not at all

accommodation.note: €315, €560 (€45, €80/night, Plovdiv boutique and Melnik estate stays)

transport.note: €330, €520 (7 days of a hired driver or a car plus daily driver hire, which is not optional here)

activities.note: €120, €220 (tasting fees, cellar tours, one vineyard lunch)

hook: Bulgaria makes wine from grapes that grow nowhere else and are named after the places that kept them. Mavrud is dark, tannic and stubborn on the plain below Plovdiv; the broad-leaved Melnik vine will only ripen in one hot sandstone valley near the Greek border. In harvest week you taste from tank, eat *kavarma* at a crush pad, sleep in a Revival house cut into a cliff, and never once get behind the wheel.

snapshot.Start / End: Plovdiv → Melnik (two bases, ~600 km with a driver)
snapshot.Getting there: Plovdiv (PDV) has limited flights; Sofia (SOF) is the practical arrival, 145 km and 1 h 45 from Plovdiv on the Trakia motorway, or 2 h by fast train. Melnik is 180 km south of Sofia on the E79 Struma motorway, 2 h 15.

itinerary.title: Plovdiv, and the food end first (arrival day)
itinerary.morning: Land at Sofia, transfer to **Plovdiv**, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and the only sane base for the Thracian Lowlands.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk the Old Town's Revival houses and the Roman theatre, then drop into **Kapana**, the former craft quarter now full of small kitchens, wine bars and bakeries. Order *banitsa* and a coffee and do nothing else.
itinerary.evening: Dinner in Kapana: *shopska salata*, *sirene po shopski*, a *grozdova rakia* before the food and a glass of Asenovgrad Mavrud with it.

itinerary.title: Brestovitsa, amphorae and the Mavrud heartland
itinerary.morning: Driver to **Brestovitsa**, twenty minutes south-west. Start at **Zagreus** for **amphora-fermented Mavrud**, clay-aged, unfined, and unlike anything else in the country. Appointment only.
itinerary.afternoon: **Todoroff** in the same village for a wider Mavrud vertical and lunch, then **Villa Yustina** at **Ustina** for their Rubin and Mavrud blends.
itinerary.evening: Back to Plovdiv. Eat lighter, *tarator* and grilled vegetables, and go to bed early, because tomorrow is the big estate.

itinerary.title: Bessa Valley and Asenovgrad
itinerary.morning: North-west to **Ognianovo** and **Bessa Valley**, the Hauptmann estate whose *Enira* labels put Bulgarian reds back on export lists. The gravity-fed winery and the barrel cellar are the tour; book weeks ahead in harvest.
itinerary.afternoon: Swing south to **Asenovgrad**, the historic capital of Mavrud, and climb to **Asen's Fortress** on its rock above the Chepelare river for the view down the vineyard plain.
itinerary.evening: Plovdiv again. A *mehana* dinner with *kavarma* in the pot and a mature Mavrud, ten years old if the list allows.

itinerary.title: East across the plain: Chirpan, Nova Zagora
itinerary.morning: Out on the Trakia motorway to **Midalidare Estate** at **Mogilovo** near Chirpan, a large, modern, appointment-only property with serious whites as well as reds.
itinerary.afternoon: On to **Rossidi** at **Nova Zagora**, a small producer known for skin-contact whites and precise Cabernet Franc, and **Château Copsa** if the timings hold. If you would rather go south-east, substitute **Katarzyna Estate** near Svilengrad on the Greek border, a longer day and appointment-only.
itinerary.evening: Return to Plovdiv. Buy *lyutenitsa* from the Central Market Hall to take home; September is when it is made.

itinerary.title: Across to the Struma and into Melnik
itinerary.morning: Leave Plovdiv, cross the Rhodope skirt to Blagoevgrad and turn south down the **E79 Struma** motorway. The landscape changes to fig, pomegranate and Mediterranean scrub.
itinerary.afternoon: Stop at **Damianitza**, near Sandanski, for the classic Melnik 55, then continue to **Melnik** itself, Bulgaria's smallest town, 200-odd inhabitants, standing under eroded **sandstone pyramids**.
itinerary.evening: The **Kordopulov House** (1754), the largest Revival house in the country, with a vast cellar tunnelled into the sandstone behind it. Taste there, then eat in the village.

itinerary.title: Villa Melnik, Rozhen and the pyramids
itinerary.morning: Up to **Villa Melnik** at **Harsovo** for a proper study of **Shiroka Melnishka Loza** against **Melnik 55** side by side, the older vine is leaner and more savoury, the selection rounder.
itinerary.afternoon: Walk or drive the ridge path to **Rozhen Monastery**, the largest in the Pirin region, then come back through the sandstone pyramids in late light.
itinerary.evening: Dinner at **Zornitza Estate** above Melnik, the most ambitious kitchen in the valley, with its own vineyard below.

itinerary.title: Orbelus, then out
itinerary.morning: **Orbelus** at **Kromidovo**, certified organic, Melnik-focused, and the clearest expression of what the Struma does without oak. Buy here; their allocations are small.
itinerary.afternoon: Lunch in **Sandanski**, then the E79 north to Sofia, two and a quarter hours.
itinerary.evening: Last dinner in Sofia. If you have a bottle of Mavrud left, this is the night for it.

accommodationStrategy.name: A boutique hotel in Plovdiv Old Town
accommodationStrategy.description: three nights in one bed with every Thracian estate inside a 90-minute radius, and Kapana's kitchens on foot at the end of each tasting day. Ask for a room off the cobbles, Old Town streets echo.
accommodationStrategy.booking: four to six weeks ahead for September and October.

accommodationStrategy.name: A guesthouse in Melnik village
accommodationStrategy.description: puts you inside the sandstone amphitheatre, walking distance from the Kordopulov cellar, so the evening tasting needs no driver at all. Family kitchens serve their own wine by the jug.
accommodationStrategy.booking: three to four weeks ahead; Melnik has very few beds.

accommodationStrategy.name: Zornitza Estate
accommodationStrategy.description: sleep on the property you are tasting at, which removes the transport problem entirely for one night, and the restaurant is the best food in the Struma.
accommodationStrategy.booking: direct with the estate, six weeks ahead in harvest.

logistics.connectivity: A1 and Yettel cover Plovdiv, Sandanski and the motorway corridor; Melnik village and the Rozhen ridge are patchy. Download offline maps for the Struma back roads.
logistics.emergency: **112**, with English-speaking operators. Plovdiv and Blagoevgrad have the nearest large hospitals; Melnik has none.
logistics.weather: The Thracian plain can still hit 35°C in early September, and the Struma is hotter still. Harvest weather is generally settled, but a Rhodope thunderstorm can shut a crush pad for a day.
logistics.bookingWindows: Appointment-only estates want **two to four weeks**, more during *grozdober*. Book the wineries first and the hotels second, cellar slots in harvest are the constraint.
logistics.money: Bulgaria has adopted the **euro**, with prices still dual-displayed in **BGN** at the fixed 1.95583 rate. Large estates take cards; village cellars, the Kordopulov House and small *mehanas* often do not. Carry €150 in cash.
logistics.transportRules: A **vignette** is required on national roads and motorways. **Do not drive and taste**, Bulgaria's enforcement is aggressive and the practical standard for this trip is zero alcohol. Hire a driver for every tasting day.
logistics.permits: No permits. Katarzyna sits in the former border zone near Svilengrad; carry your passport there. Duty-free allowances out of the EU are the limit on what you can carry home.

proTips: Book Bessa Valley, Zagreus and Katarzyna before you book anything else. They are appointment-only, they cap group sizes, and in harvest they close to visitors on picking days at no notice.
Ask at every cellar for *"vino ot tank"*, wine from tank. During *grozdober* winemakers will pull fermenting Mavrud with a pipette, and that is the taste you came for.
Order **Melnik 55 and Shiroka Melnishka Loza side by side** at Villa Melnik and pay for the extra glass. The difference between the selection and the original vine is the whole story of the Struma.
Buy *lyutenitsa* and *sirene* at Plovdiv's Central Market Hall in the third week of September, when the roasted-pepper smell fills the street outside.
Say *"grozdova"* or *"slivova"* when you order *rakia*. Asking by fruit signals you know the difference and usually gets you the homemade bottle from under the bar.
Stay in Melnik village rather than Sandanski. It is smaller, quieter, and the cellar tastings become a walk instead of a transfer.
Use the estates' own drivers where they offer them. Bessa Valley, Villa Melnik and Zornitza can all arrange transport, and it is often cheaper than a full-day city hire.

raw.The appellations: Two PGIs cover nearly everything you will drink. **Thracian Lowlands PGI** (*Тракийска низина*) runs east from Plovdiv across the Maritsa plain to the Turkish border, hot days, cool nights off the Rhodopes, and the home of Mavrud. **Struma Valley PGI** (*Долината на Струма*) is a narrow, Mediterranean-influenced corridor in the far south-west, hemmed by Pirin and the Greek frontier, and it is the only place in Bulgaria where the broad-leaved Melnik vine reliably ripens. A third, the **Danubian Plain PGI** in the north-west, is Gamza country and off this route.
raw.The native grapes, correctly: **Mavrud**, late-ripening, deeply coloured, high tannin, at its best around **Asenovgrad and Brestovitsa**; ages ten years and needs food. **Rubin**, a Bulgarian crossing of **Nebbiolo × Syrah** bred at the Pleven institute, giving perfume and structure and often blended with Mavrud. **Shiroka Melnishka Loza**, the broad-leaved Melnik vine, thin-skinned, high-acid, savoury, and so late that it only finishes ripening in the Struma. **Melnik 55**, an earlier-ripening selection from it, softer and more approachable. **Dimyat**, a crisp white of the east. **Red Misket** (*Cherven Misket*), aromatic, from around Sungurlare and Karlovo. **Gamza** in the north-west, light and sour-cherry, worth ordering if you see it.
raw.Producers, and who to ask for: Thracian Lowlands: **Bessa Valley** at **Ognianovo**, founded by **Karl-Heinz Hauptmann** with Stephan von Neipperg, the estate that proved Bulgaria could make serious Bordeaux-styled reds; **Villa Yustina** at Ustina; **Zagreus** at Brestovitsa, whose **amphora-fermented Mavrud** is the country's most interesting single wine; **Todoroff**, also at Brestovitsa, the most visitor-ready cellar in the region; **Midalidare Estate** at Mogilovo near Chirpan; **Rossidi** at Nova Zagora, small and experimental; **Château Copsa**; and **Katarzyna Estate**, hard against the Greek border near Svilengrad. Struma Valley: **Villa Melnik** at Harsovo; **Orbelus** at Kromidovo, certified organic and Melnik-focused; **Damianitza** at Damyanitsa near Sandanski, the old cooperative reborn; and **Zornitza Estate** above Melnik, which is also a hotel and restaurant.
raw.Appointment-only, flag these clearly: **Bessa Valley, Zagreus, Katarzyna, Rossidi, Midalidare and Château Copsa are strictly by prior appointment.** Katarzyna in particular is a working border-zone estate and does not take walk-ins. **Todoroff, Villa Melnik, Orbelus and Zornitza** keep more regular tasting-room hours but still prefer a booking, especially during harvest.
raw.Signature dishes, with their names: *Shopska salata*, tomato, cucumber, roasted pepper, raw onion, grated white brine cheese, and the national dish by adoption. *Tarator*, cold cucumber, yoghurt, garlic, dill and walnut soup, served in a bowl or a glass. *Kavarma*, slow-cooked pork or chicken with peppers and onion, baked and served in its clay pot. *Sirene po shopski*, brine cheese baked in a pot with tomato, pepper and an egg cracked on top. *Banitsa*, coiled filo with *sirene* and egg, eaten for breakfast. *Lyutenitsa*, the roasted pepper, tomato and aubergine relish that every household makes in September.
raw.*Rakia*, and the distinction that matter: *Rakia* is fruit brandy, usually 40% and often much more when homemade. **Grozdova rakia** is distilled from grapes, cleaner, sharper, the standard aperitif with *shopska salata*. **Slivova rakia** is from plums, rounder, sweeter, the north-western and Balkan-foothill style. Ordering "rakia" without specifying gets you whatever the house has. *Muskatova* is a fragrant grape variant worth asking for.
raw.Drinking and driving: Bulgaria polices drink-driving hard and the only workable rule on a tasting trip is **zero tolerance**. **A hired driver is mandatory**, budget €80, €120 a day for a car and driver, or use estate-arranged transfers. Police checks on the Trakia and Struma motorways are routine.
